Partially compared with BI 298 (rep-1973-4) == Parāśara Smṛti == =The Section on Conduct (Ācāra-kāṇḍa)=
The Conduct of the Four Castes (Cāturvarṇyācāra): Now, therefore, on the summit of the Himālaya mountain, in the abode of the Devadāru forest,
the sages of old questioned Vyāsa as he sat with one-pointed concentration.
"In this current Kali age, tell us the dharma that is beneficial for human beings,
as well as the rules of purification and conduct exactly as they are— O son of Satyavatī."
Having heard those words of the sage, he— accompanied by his disciples, resembling the sun in brilliance,
possessed of great luster, and expert in the Śrutis and Smṛtis— replied.
"I am not an omniscient knower of all principles; how then could I speak on dharma?
My father alone should be questioned," thus Vyāsa spoke to his son.
Then all those sages, desiring to know the true meaning of dharma,
placed the sage Vyāsa at their head and went to the hermitage of Badarikā.
It is strewn with various beautiful flowers, adorned with fruit-bearing trees,
endowed with rivers and springs, and graced by sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
Abounding with the cries of wild beasts and birds, surrounded by the abodes of deities,
and adorned with the dances and songs of yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
In that assembly of sages, [he saw] Parāśara,
the son of Śakti, seated at ease, possessed of great splendor, and surrounded by a host of preeminent munis.
Having joined his palms in the añjali gesture, Vyāsa, together with the sages,
honored him with circumambulations, salutations, and hymns of praise.
Then, with a heart full of contentment, the great sage Parāśara, that bull among sages, sat down and said, "Welcome; speak."
Having said, "It is well; it is right," Vyāsa immediately asked:
"O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, if you have any affection for me, [tell me] out of love if you know [this]."
"O father, tell me the Dharma, for I am worthy of your grace.
I have heard the Dharmas of Manu, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa."
The Gārgya, Gautama, and Uśanasa Smṛtis; likewise those of Atri, Viṣṇu, Saṃvarta, Dakṣa, and Aṅgiras.
From Śātātapa and Hārīta, likewise from Yājñavalkya,
as well as the Dharmas composed by Āpastamba, Śaṅkha, and Likhita.
"O Sage, these [works] composed by Kātyāyana as well as those of the sage Prācetasa have indeed been heard by me;
having been spoken by you, their meaning has not been forgotten."
In this Manvantara, throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā,
all dharmas were born in the Kṛta age and all have perished in the Kali age.
Speak briefly on the common conduct of the four castes—
that which must be performed by those learned in dharma belonging to all four varṇas.
"Speak at length, O knower of the true nature of Dharma, concerning both its subtle and gross aspects.
At the conclusion of Vyāsa's words, Parāśara, the foremost of sages, [replied].
He has declared the determination of Dharma, both subtle and gross, in detail. Listen, my son, I shall speak; and let the sages likewise listen.
In every kalpa, through their destruction and rebirth, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśvara are always the determiners of the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous.
No one is the author of the Veda; rather, the four-faced Brahmā, having remembered the Veda, likewise remembers the Dharmas at the end of each Kalpa, just as Manu does in every interval.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are one thing; in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages they are another;
and in the Kali age they are yet another, according to the nature of each respective age.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone is supreme.
In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu are prescribed; in the Tretā, those of Gautama; in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, the Smṛti of Parāśara is prescribed.
In the Kṛta age one should abandon the country; in the Tretā age, one should abandon the village;
in the Dvāpara age, one should abandon the single family; but in the Kali age, one should abandon only the perpetrator.
In the Kṛta age, one falls [from dharma] merely by conversing [with an outcaste]; in the Tretā, by touching him;
in the Dvāpara, by taking his food; but in the Kali age, one falls through performing his work.
In the Kṛta age, the curse takes effect immediately; in the Tretā, after ten days;
in the Dvāpara, after one month; but in the Kali age, after one year.
A gift is given by approaching [the recipient] in the Kṛta age; in the Tretā, it is given after being summoned;
in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali age, it is given through service.
Giving after approaching [the recipient] is the highest; giving after merely calling out [to him] is middling; giving to one who asks is low; but giving as a result of service is fruitless.
In the Kali age, dharma is indeed conquered by adharma, truth by falsehood,
kings by thieves, and men by women.
In this Kali age, the Agnihotra sacrifices constantly fall into neglect, reverence for one's guru is abandoned, and young girls give birth [to children] prematurely.
In the Kṛta age, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā, they reside in the flesh;
in the Dvāpara, in the blood; and in the Kali age, they reside in food and other such things.

One should not engage in the censure of those duties that exist in each respective age, nor of those twice-born ones who exist in each respective place; for those twice-born ones are indeed the very forms of the ages.
In each age, however, the capacity [of beings] is different, as described by the sages;
and the expiation (prāyaścitta) has also been declared by Parāśara and is now prescribed.
"Recalling all of that this very day, I speak it to you:
O preeminent sages, listen to the conduct of the four castes."
The doctrine of Parāśara is meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin;
it was conceived for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas and for the establishment of Dharma.
For all four castes, conduct is the protector of dharma;
for those whose bodies have fallen away from conduct, dharma turns its back on them.
A Brāhmaṇa who is constantly devoted to the six duties, who worships the deities and guests, and who eats only the remnants of the oblation, does not come to grief.
The twilight ritual bath, silent recitation, burnt offerings, worship of the deities and guests,
hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice— these are the six duties to be performed day after day.
Whether he is liked or disliked, whether he is a fool or even a scholar,
whoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite is a guest who brings about the attainment of heaven.
One should recognize as a guest (atithi) a person who has arrived from a long journey and is exhausted, appearing at the time of the Vaiśvadeva offering; one who arrives before that is not a guest.
One should never accept as a guest someone from one's own village;
because he arrives without a fixed time, he is therefore called an *atithi* (guest).
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and so forth,
by offering water for the hands (*arghya*), a seat, and by washing his feet.
A householder should generate affection by giving food with faith, by responding to pleasant inquiries, and by following one who is departing.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
the ancestors of that person do not eat for fifteen years.
If a guest goes away with unfulfilled expectations, the fire-oblation performed by that host— despite his thousand loads of wood and his hundred jars of ghee— is useless.
One should sow seed in a good field and bestow wealth upon a worthy recipient;
for what is sown and given in a good field and a worthy recipient does not perish.
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, Vedic school, sacred study, or learning;
rather, one should conceive of the deity within one's heart, for he embodies all the gods.
Just as a Brahmin who observes excellent vows is unprecedented [in merit], and likewise one who is an extraordinary guest,
so too those two— who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas— are unprecedented [in merit] day after day.
When the Vaiśvadeva rite has commenced and a mendicant has arrived at the house,
one should set aside a portion for the Vaiśvadeva and then dismiss the mendicant.
Both the ascetic and the student are the rightful owners of cooked food.
Having eaten without first giving food to those two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should give three portions of alms to the wandering mendicant and the student;
thereafter, if one has the means, one may give as much as desired without restriction.
One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, then give the alms-food, and again give water;
that alms-food is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is comparable to the ocean.
He who possesses a parasol, a horse, an elephant, and a prosperous retinue of attendants shall occupy the station of Indra; therefore, one should not dispute his authority.
A mendicant is able to remove the sin committed during the Vaiśvadeva rite;
however, the Vaiśvadeva rite does not remove the faults committed by the mendicant.
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite—
know that all of them are fruitless and fall quickly into an impure hell.
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and excluded from hospitality—
all of them go to hell and enter the womb of a crow.
Whether he be a sinner, an outcaste, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a murderer of his father—
if such a person arrives when the Vaiśvadeva rite has commenced, he is a guest who leads one to heaven.
He who eats with his head wrapped, he who eats facing south,
or he who places his hand on his left foot— verily, the *rakṣas* consume that food.
The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms while remaining without vows and unlearned; for such a village provides sustenance to thieves.
For the Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and wielding the rod of punishment,
should conquer the enemy armies and protect the earth according to Dharma.
One should pluck flower after flower, but should not cause the roots to be cut; one should act like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-burner.
Acquiring wealth, dealing in gems, the protection of cattle,
agriculture, and trade are declared to be the occupations of a Vaiśya. For a Śūdra, the supreme duty is said to be service to the twice-born.
If one performs anything otherwise than prescribed, that shall become fruitless for him.
Salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—these do not become defiled for those of the Śūdra caste; one may sell all of these.
By selling honey or meat, by eating what is forbidden to eat,
or by having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his status at that very moment.
By drinking the milk of a *kapilā* cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Veda, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla. Henceforth, [I shall describe] the ritual duties and conduct of a householder in the Kali age.
One should practice with one's ability the common dharma pertaining to the four castes and stages of life.
I shall first declare that according to the words of Parāśara:
a Brahmin, while engaged in the six duties, may also perform the work of agriculture.
One should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted.
A Brahmin should not drive an ox that is deficient in limb, diseased, or impotent.
One should drive a bull that has steady limbs, is strong, well-fed, and well-neighing, but devoid of castrated bulls, for half the day; thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath.
One should practice the recitation of mantras (*japya*), the worship of deities (*devārcana*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the study of sacred texts (*svādhyāya*).
A twice-born man should feed one, two, three,
or four *snātaka* Brahmins with grains earned by his own labor on land tilled by himself.
One should perform the five sacrifices and cause the initiation for a sacrifice to be carried out.
One who sells sesame seeds, liquids, or salt is equal to one who sells grain;
such is the livelihood of a Brahmin, as is the selling of grass, wood, and the like.
If a Brāhmaṇa should practice agriculture, he incurs a great fault;
the sin that a fisherman incurs in a year, he incurs in a single day.
One who strikes with an iron-pointed wooden stick is a *lāṅgalī*;
likewise, one who uses a noose is a fisherman, and one who kills with arrows is a hunter or a fowler.
The donor and the cultivator alike—these are all equal sharers [of the merit].
Having cut down trees, having broken the earth, and having killed worms and insects...
A farmer is liberated from all sins by the sacrifice of the threshing floor,
provided that he does not fail to give to the twice-born when he has arrived at the root of his wealth.
"He is a thief, he is most sinful— one should designate him as a slayer of a Brahmin—
having given a sixth part to the king and a twenty-first part to the gods."
By giving a thirtieth part of [the merit] to Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins.
A Kṣatriya also, having engaged in agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins.
A Vaiśya and likewise a Śūdra should engage in agriculture, trade, and the arts;
those Śūdras who perform improper acts are abandoned by the twice-born because they fail to serve them.
They indeed become short-lived and undoubtedly go to hell.
This is the eternal dharma for all four castes as well.
Therefore, I shall now declare the purification regarding birth and likewise death:
Brāhmaṇas become pure after three days in the case of both a funeral and a birth-impurity.
A Kṣatriya is purified in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days,
and a Śūdra becomes pure in one month, according to the words of Parāśara.
In the case of attending upon Brahmins, however, purification of the limbs occurs;
but in the case of the birth of Brahmins or touching a deity, it is ordained [that the entire body be purified].
A Brahmin is purified by ten days in the case of birth; a Kṣatriya, by twelve days;
a Vaiśya, by fifteen days; and a Śūdra becomes pure after a month.
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and is well-versed in the Vedas is purified in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days, while one devoid of both is purified in ten days.
One who has fallen away from [proper] birth and conduct, who is devoid of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyopāsana*),
and who is a Brahmin in name only, shall remain impure for ten days.
Those who share a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) are heirs, even if they have separate wives and dwellings;
upon their birth or death, the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka) shall belong to them.
That impurity (sūtaka) remains within the lineage until the fourth person;
however, the fifth descendant born of one's own line incurs the severance of inheritance.
In the fourth [generation], there shall be ten nights; in the case of a male in the fifth, six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days.
In the case of death by leaping from a precipice or by fire, as well as when one has died in another country,
and when a child has died or one has renounced the world (become a *saṃnyāsin*), immediate purification is ordained.
If it is heard that someone of the same lineage (sagotra) has died in another country,
one becomes pure by bathing immediately after observing either three nights, one day and night, or [simply] bathing at once.
If a Brahmin who has gone to another country dies due to exhaustion caused by time,
and his body is destroyed such that the date of death is not known;
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on whichever is the eleventh day of the dark fortnight—
one should perform the offering of water, the presentation of rice-balls, and the Śrāddha ceremony there.
For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and those who have just emerged from the womb,
there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water libations.
If the fetus should perish or be miscarried by a woman,
the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had been situated.

Until the fourth month, it shall be a miscarriage (srāva); in the fifth and sixth months, it is a birth (pāta). Beyond that, it is a full delivery (prasūti), and there shall be ten days of impurity (sūtaka).
When one who has teethed, one who has been born after [the death of an elder], or one for whom the *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed passes away,
there shall be impurity for three nights for those performing the cremation rites.

Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is said to be one night; until the instruction for the vows (vratādeśa), it is three nights; and beyond that, it is ten nights.
For those whose householders maintain a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) and in whose home the sacrificial fire is offered,
there shall be no impurity (sūtaka) arising from contact with them.
A Brahmin becomes defiled by contact during both birth and death;
however, for one who has withdrawn from such contact, there is neither impurity due to death nor impurity due to birth.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female and male slaves, and barbers—
as well as kings and those learned in the Vedas— are proclaimed to be immediately pure.
A twice-born man who maintains his vows, one purified by a sacrificial session (satra), and one who has established the sacred fires—
there is no birth-impurity for these, nor for the king, if the monarch so desires.
When a Brahmin who has been invited is intent on giving away his wealth or is afflicted by illness at the time of death,
the sages have declared that he becomes pure according to the prescribed time.
But if the householder does not cause a confusion of castes during childbirth,
the mother becomes pure after ten days, while the father is pure immediately upon bathing.

For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death; however, for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (*upaspṛśya*).
If a twice-born man has sexual intercourse with his wife while she is in childbirth, impurity (sūtaka) shall indeed affect him,
even if he is a Brahmin learned in the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍ-aṅga).
"From association, fault arises; for there is no other fault in a twice-born man.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid association with every effort."
In the case of marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, even if a death or birth impurity occurs in the interval,
there is no fault in giving away wealth that was previously intended for the purpose.
If death or birth occurs again within ten days,
the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that [subsequent] period has not yet reached ten days.
For those who have perished for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as for those killed while rescuing a prisoner or a cow,
and for those who have perished in battles, there is impurity for one night.
These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and he who is slain while facing the enemy in battle.
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided that he does not utter words of cowardice.
Upon seeing a Brahmin who has renounced the world (saṃnyasta), the sun moves from its place:
"Having pierced my orb, he shall proceed to the supreme abode."
But he who, when the armies have been broken and are fleeing in every direction,
comes as their protector, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
The daughters of the gods carry away and delight that hero whose body has been wounded by arrows, mallets, or staffs.
Thousands of celestial women run forward in haste toward a hero slain in battle, each crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine!"
O Brahmins, those seekers of heaven who attain it through multitudes of sacrifices and through austerity reach that place only after time;
however, heroes who abandon their lives in a noble battle reach it in an instant.
By victory one obtains fortune; even by death, one gains celestial nymphs. Since this body perishes in an instant, what anxiety can there be regarding death in battle?
When blood flows from the forehead and enters the mouth during battle,
that is indeed seen to be equal to the drinking of Soma in the sacrifice of war, performed according to the prescribed rules.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain,
in successive order, the fruit of a sacrifice at every step.
For those who perform auspicious deeds, there is no inauspiciousness or sin whatsoever;
for them, immediate purification is ordained simply by immersion in water.
Having carried and cremated a deceased person who was destitute, friendless, and of the highest twice-born caste, one becomes pure by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Having followed a deceased kinsman or even a non-kinsman at his own request,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a deceased Kṣatriya out of ignorance,
he remains impure for one day and is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a corpse out of ignorance— whether it be that of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra—
he shall observe impurity for two nights and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse as it is being carried away, he shall remain impure for three nights. (Parāśara Smṛti 3.45)

When three nights have thus elapsed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he becomes purified by consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

When a Śūdra, having been turned away [from the funeral procession], stands at the edge of the water, he should then be followed by the twice-born; this is the eternal law. (Parāśara Smṛti 3.47ab–cd) [Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa]
Whether it be a woman or a man, if they should commit [suicide] out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or even fear, this course of action is prescribed [as follows].
He sinks into blinding darkness filled with pus and blood;
for sixty thousand years, he enters hell.
One should not cause impurity, nor water, nor fire, nor the shedding of tears;
likewise, the carriers [of the body], the givers of fire, and those who cut the noose.
"Prajāpati has declared that those [who have killed a cow] are purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance—
this applies to one who has killed a cow, as well as one who has hanged herself, or one who was caused to be killed by a Brāhmaṇa."
But those Brahmins who touch [the corpse], those who carry it, those who provide the fire,
others who follow it, and those who cut the ropes— [they all become impure].
They become purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance; they should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a learned Brāhmaṇa.
For three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk;
for three days one should drink hot clarified butter, and for three days one should subsist on air alone.
One should drink six palas of water, then three palas of milk, and then one pala of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the *tapta-kṛcchra* penance.
If a Brahmin should, unintentionally, associate with those who have fallen [from their caste] and others, he should observe a penance for five days,
ten days, or even twelve days.
For one month, half a month, or one month, or even two months; for half a year, a year, or one year, or beyond that, he becomes equal to him.
In the first fortnight, one should observe a three-night fast; in the second, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance;
and in the third fortnight, one should perform the *sāṃtapana kṛcchra*.
On the fourth day, there shall be a ten-night penance; on the fifth, a parāka is prescribed.
On the sixth, one should perform a cāndrāyaṇa, and on the seventh, two aindavas.
For the sake of purification, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months during the eighth [period];
the number of *suvarṇas* as the measure of the fortnights shall be the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
But that woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband,
goes to hell after death and becomes a widow again and again.
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of foeticide; there is no doubt in this matter.
She who disregards her husband— whether he be poor, diseased, or foolish—
is born as a bitch after death, and again and again as a sow.
If a woman, while her husband is still living, observes a fast or performs a vow,
she takes away the life-span of her husband and that woman shall go to hell.
"If a woman performs a vow without even having asked her husband's permission, all of that shall go to the Rākṣasas; thus Manu has declared."
But she who commits misconduct toward her kinsmen or those of the same caste,
or she who causes an abortion— one should never speak with her.
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin, that same sin is doubled in the destruction of a fetus;
there shall be no atonement for her, for her abandonment is ordained.
Neither by his household nor again by his *agnihotra* does he become [pure];
he who is averse to dharma becomes a *karmacāṇḍāla*.
If seed brought by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone's field, that owner of the field receives the crop;
the owner of the seed does not deserve a share.
Similarly, two types of sons born of another's wife are recorded in the tradition as the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*:
the *kuṇḍa* is one born while the husband is still living, and the *golaka* is one born when the husband is dead.
The legitimate son (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the adopted son (datta), and the son made (kṛtrima)—
whom the mother or the father may give away, he becomes an adopted son (dattaka).

The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, the younger brother who marries before his elder, the woman with whom such a marriage is contracted, the giver [of the bride], and the officiating priest— all these go to hell.
For the elder brother who marries before his younger brother (parivitti), there are two *kṛcchra* penances; for the maiden, one *kṛcchra*;
for the giver, a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*; and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] in the case of those who are humpbacked, dwarfs, eunuchs, stammerers, or mentally dull, nor in the case of those who are blind from birth, deaf, or mute.
The son of a paternal uncle, the son of a stepmother, and likewise the son of another's wife—
there is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] for the purpose of uniting with a wife, the sacred fire, and the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
When the elder brother is present, one should not perform the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) at all;
however, with his permission, one may do so, according to the word of Śaṅkha.
"When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste— under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women."
When her husband has died, the woman who remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy attains heaven upon her death, just as those lifelong students of the Veda do.
There are thirty-five million hairs on a human being;
for as long as that duration she who follows her husband shall dwell in heaven.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
even so a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoices together with him.
But that best of the twice-born who is bitten by wolves, dogs, jackals, or the like—
Having bathed, one should mutter the Gāyatrī, the purifier, the mother of the Vedas.
A bath with water from the horns of cows at the confluence of two great rivers,
or even by beholding the ocean, shall purify one bitten by a dog.
If a twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies and vows is bitten by a dog,
he becomes pure by bathing with water containing gold and consuming clarified butter.
But one who, while observing his vows, has been bitten by a dog should fast for three nights;
having drunk ghee mixed with water containing *kuśa* grass, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
Whether he be without vows or even with vows, if a twice-born man is bitten by a dog,
he becomes purified by prostrating himself and being gazed upon by Brahmins with their eyes.
For that which has been smelled, sniffed, licked, or scratched with the nails,
cleansing with water and heating with fire are prescribed.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman is bitten by a jackal, a wolf, or a dog,
she becomes pure immediately upon seeing the risen planets and stars.
When the moon is never visible during the dark fortnight,
one should look toward whichever direction the moon has gone.
In a village where no Brāhmaṇas reside, if a distinguished twice-born man is bitten by a dog,
he becomes pure immediately after bathing and circumambulating a bull.
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is struck by a Caṇḍāla, a dog-cooker, cattle, or other Brahmins,
or if he dies from poison or commits suicide;
A Brahmin shall burn that Brahmin in the world-fire (loka-agni) without the recitation of mantras;
and having touched him, carried his bier, or burned him, one is purified in every way by performing the same rites for all the sapinda relatives.
Afterwards, at the instruction of the Brahmins, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having taken the burnt bones again, the twice-born man should wash them with milk.
One should cremate [the body] again with one's own fire, independently and separately for each.
If a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) departs on a journey when the time [for his funeral rites] has arrived, [he should be so cremated].
O bulls among sages, listen to the ritual for the deceased Agnihotra, for the fire of one who has met with the destruction of the body remains in his house.
Having spread out a black antelope skin and fashioned the form of a man with *kuśa* grass, one should [place] six hundred and one palāśa leaves along with their stalks.
One should place forty [beads] on the head, one hundred on the neck;
one should place one hundred on the two arms, and ten indeed on the fingers.
One should place one hundred [strokes] on the buttocks, and likewise two hundred on the abdomen;
one should place eight on the testicles and five on the penis.
One should give twenty-one [parts] for the two thighs, two hundred for the knees and shanks, and six for the toes of the feet; thereafter, one should place the sacrificial vessels.
Having placed the *samyā* on the penis and the *araṇī* between the testicles,
one should place the *juhū* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left.
One should place a mortar on the ear and set a pestle on the back;
having cast a grinding stone upon the chest, one should place rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds in the mouth.
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel at the two ears and the *ājya-sthalī* (clarified butter vessel) at the two eyes;
one should place fragments of gold in the ears, the eyes, the mouth, and the nose.
One should place all the implements of the *agnihotra* there without exception, and offer a single oblation once, saying: "To this one for the heavenly world, svāhā! (ParSm 5.22).
The son, or a brother, or even another kinsman should perform the cremation rite; the wise should carry out the funeral rites in this manner.
One should perform such a rite as this; it is traditionally taught that it leads to the world of Brahmā.
Those twice-born who cremate him in this manner attain the supreme goal.
Those who perform an action otherwise than prescribed, impelled by their own arbitrary notions,
become short-lived and indeed fall into a foul hell.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the killing of living beings.
And also the extensive exposition on the meaning of Manu’s verses as previously stated by Parāśara.
Having eaten the meat of a curlew, a crane, a swan, a ruddy goose, a cock,
or a web-footed bird, as well as a śarabha, one is purified in a day and a night.
Even the crane and the lapwing, as well as the parrot and the pigeon, and the snake, the crocodile,
and the vighāti, are purified by eating only at night.
One who kills wolves, crows, pigeons, śāris,
or partridges is purified by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water during both twilights.
The killer of vultures, hawks, cranes,
or owls shall subsist on uncooked food for one day, remaining standing and consuming only air during the three periods of the day.
By eating at night, one is purified by abstaining from food for those who eat at night, as well as for the valguṇī, the ṭiṭṭibha, the kokila, the khañjarītaka, the lāvika, and those with red wings.
Having killed a kāraṇḍava, a cakora, a piṅgalā, a kurara,
or a bhāradvāja and others, one becomes purified by worshipping Śiva.
For eating the flesh of the bheruṇḍa, the cāṣa, the bhāsa, the pigeon, and the kapiñjala,
as well as for eating the meat of all other birds, there shall be a fast for one day and night.
Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a *ḍuṇḍubha* [water-snake], one should feed *kṛsara* (rice and sesame) to Brahmins; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is an iron staff.
Having killed a porcupine, a mongoose, a monitor lizard, a tortoise, or a porcupine-scaled fish,
as well as one who eats eggplant, one becomes pure after a day and a night.
One who kills a wolf, a jackal, a bear, a hyena, a dog,
or a killer [of livestock] should give a prastha of sesame seeds to a twice-born man and subsist on air for three days.
For the killing of an elephant, a fourfold army, a buffalo, or a camel,
the penance is one day and night, with immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
By killing a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger,
one is purified in three nights by means of the libation of water (tarpaṇa) for Brahmins.
The killer of a deer, a female deer, a boar, a sheep,
or a goat shall fast for a day and night and eat only food that has not been ploughed by a furrow.
In this same manner, for all four-footed animals that roam the forest,
one should remain standing for a day and night, reciting the Jātavedas hymns.
If one should cause the death of an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman,
he shall perform two Prājāpatya penances and give eleven bulls as a sacrificial fee.
If one should cause injury to a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya who is free from fault,
he too shall perform two Kṛcchra penances and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee.
Having killed a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who is devoted to sacred rites, or an excellent twice-born man who is engaged in improper acts,
one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give thirty cows as a sacrificial fee.
If someone has killed a Caṇḍāla near a Brāhmaṇa,
he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee.
Whether it be a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even another [lower caste],
when the death penalty for a Caṇḍāla has been incurred, one is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance.
If a thief, a dog-cooker, or a Caṇḍāla is struck by a Brāhmaṇa,
he becomes pure after staying overnight and bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a thief, a dog-cooker, or a Caṇḍāla should be struck by a Brahmin,
he becomes pure by staying overnight and bathing, and then consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one has slept together with Caṇḍālas, one should fast for three nights;
having traveled along a path shared with a Caṇḍāla, one becomes pure by recollecting the Gāyatrī.
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun;
upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
If an elder brother drinks water from a well or a step-well dug by a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance, he becomes pure after a day and a night of eating only one meal.
Having drunk water from a well that has been touched by the vessel of a Caṇḍāla,
one attains purification after three nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (yāvaka).
If a twice-born man drinks water that has been contained in a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he who discards it immediately should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If one does not offer water for him whose body is still digesting [food], a Prājāpatya penance should not be assigned; rather, he should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra.
A Brahmin should perform the Sāṃtapana penance, and a Kṣatriya the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya should perform half of that, and a Śūdra should perform a quarter of it.

If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk contained in a vessel belonging to those of the lowest castes (antyaja), [he must undergo penance].
For the twice-born, expiation is by means of the Brahmakūrca penance and fasting;
for a Śūdra, it is by fasting and likewise by giving gifts according to his capacity.
O best of the twice-born, if one should ever eat the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance,
he becomes pure after ten nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
One should eat a single morsel each day of cow’s urine and barley gruel;
this is declared to be the vow for one who remains under restraint for ten days.
But where a Caṇḍāla stays in a house without being known, the twice-born perform a rite of favor for one who has approached them once he is known. (ParSm 6.34)
Those who have mastered the Vedas and know the Dharma, chanting the teachings that issued from the mouth of the Sage,
shall rescue him as he falls from the confusion of sin.
One should eat curd, clarified butter, milk, cow’s urine,
and barley-gruel together with all [the others], and perform immersion at the three junctions of the day.
For three days he should eat with curd, for three days he should eat with clarified butter,
and for three days he should eat with milk— consuming each one for a period of three days.
One should not eat food that is corrupted by one's state of mind, nor that which is leftover, nor that defiled by insects;
however, three palas of curd and milk, and one pala of ghee [may be consumed].
Purification for both copper and bell-metal is accomplished by means of ash;
for garments, by means of washing with water; and for earthenware, by means of discarding it.
Having placed safflower, molasses, cotton, salt, oil,
and ghee at the door, one should place grain and fire within the house.
Thus purified, he should thereafter perform the libation for the Brahmins;
he should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the learned Brahmins.
It becomes pure again by means of plastering, digging, fire-offerings, and recitation;
furthermore, for Brahmins, no defect of the ground exists when it serves as a foundation.
If one has contact with Caṇḍālas for a month or even for half a month,
one becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (yāvaka).
A washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter, or a basket-maker—
if she remains in the house of one belonging to the four castes unrecognized— then [she may be taken].
Having ascertained the expiation, however, one should perform even half of what was previously stated;
one should not set fire to the house, but should cause all the rest to be performed.
If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone's house,
he must be expelled from that dwelling, and the earthenware vessels must be discarded.
One should never discard a vessel that is full of liquid;
likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
If a worm should arise from the opening of a wound of a Brāhmaṇa when pus and blood have formed there, what should be the expiation for him?
Having been defiled by worms, one becomes pure by bathing and drinking cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter for three days.
A Kṣatriya, having given five māṣas of gold, should likewise prescribe a cow as the sacrificial fee for a Vaiśya and a fast.
For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra becomes pure through giving alone.
The statement "It is without flaw," which the gods of the earth (Brāhmaṇas) utter.
Having bowed with one's head, it should be accepted, for that indeed yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whatever defect there may be in recitation, whatever defect in austerity, and whatever defect in the performance of sacrificial rites—[all these are remedied by this].
Everything provided by Brāhmaṇas becomes faultless,
even in times of disease, calamity, exhaustion, famine, or likewise during a violent upheaval.
Fasting, vows, and burnt offerings are indeed to be performed by the twice-born;
or else, the Brahmins, being satisfied, bestow grace upon everything.
In this world, one attains all desires through [gifts] prepared by the twice-born;
likewise, favor is prescribed for the weak, as well as for children and the elderly.
Otherwise, there would be a fault; therefore, it is not considered a favor.
[This applies] whether out of affection, greed, fear, or even ignorance.
But those who show favor [to such a person] incur that very sin;
for they speak of a restrictive rule [as permissible] when the destruction of the body has arrived.
One should never perform [an act] while healthy if it obstructs a great duty;
those fools who do so while healthy speak what is contrary to the rule.
Those who, having themselves undertaken a vow, treat a Brāhmaṇa with contempt, become the creators of obstacles for him and fall quickly into an impure hell.
His fast would be in vain, and he would not be endowed with merit;
that very rule alone should be accepted if even a single twice-born man should so declare.
One should not speak contrary to the words of the twice-born, for otherwise one becomes a killer of an embryo;
the Brāhmaṇas are a moving sacred ford, for the virtuous are indeed the embodiments of sacred fords.
By the mere water [consecrated] by their words, even defiled people are purified;
whatever the Brāhmaṇas speak, the gods consider that to be authoritative.
A Brahmin embodies all the gods; his word is never otherwise.
Fasting, religious vows, ritual bathing, pilgrimage to sacred fords, recitation of mantras, and austerity [all derive their power from him].
The fruit belongs entirely to him for whom the rite has been performed by a Brahmin. When food and the like are infested with insects or defiled by flies or hair, [one should act accordingly].
If one touches water during that interval, one should touch that food with ashes;
likewise, a Brahmin who, while eating, touches his foot with his hand [should do the same].
He eats his own leavings from a vessel that has been left in his hand;
he should not eat while standing on footrests, nor while seated upon a couch.
One should avoid eating while being looked at by a dog or a caṇḍāla;
likewise, one should avoid food that is prohibited and observe the purification of such food.
Just as it was spoken by Parāśara, so do I speak to you:
food that has been cooked in a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* measure, if it has been defiled by crows or dogs—
"By what is this purified?"—thus one should inquire of the Brāhmaṇas.
However, food that has been pecked at by crows or licked by dogs, if it amounts to a *droṇa*, should not be discarded.
By Brahmins who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*) and who uphold the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*),
thirty-two *prasthas* are recorded as one *droṇa*, and two *prasthas* as one *āḍhaka*.
Thereafter, those who know the Śruti and Smṛti understand that food measuring one droṇa or one āḍhaka is purified if it has been licked by a crow or a dog,
or smelled by a cow or a donkey.

A Brahmin should discard even a very small amount of food; purification occurs when [the quantity] is one *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka*. Having removed from the food that portion which has been defiled by saliva, [the remainder may be consumed].
Having sprinkled the water with gold, one should heat it with the remnant of the oblation;
[the ordeal is considered valid when] touched by both the remnant of the oblation and the water containing gold.
"By the chanting of the Veda by Brahmins, that food becomes pure at that very moment.
But if there is oil or even cow's milk there, how can purity be achieved?"

In that case, one should discard a small amount [of the substance] by means of purifying the oil and by the flame of fire; the purification of cow's milk is thus prescribed. (This is the purification of substances.)
Now, therefore, the purification of substances according to the words of Parāśara: the purification of wooden vessels is held to be by planing.
Bell-metal is purified by ashes, and copper is purified by acid; a woman who does not engage in intercourse is purified by her menses.
One is purified by the current of a river if no [signs of] defilement are seen;
likewise, when step-wells, wells, or ponds have been somehow defiled.
Having drawn out a hundred jars [of water], one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
A girl of eight years is a *Gaurī*, while one of nine years is a *Rohiṇī*.
A girl becomes a *kanyā* (a maiden eligible for marriage) until she reaches ten years of age; beyond that, she is *rajasvalā* (menstruating).
But when the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter [is at fault].
Month after month, her own ancestors— the mother, the father, and likewise the eldest brother— themselves drink her menstrual blood.
These three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses: the one who would marry such a girl, and the Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by passion, weds her.

Indeed, that Brahmin who serves a *vṛṣalī* becomes unfit for conversation and excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkteya*) by merely spending a single night with her; such a twice-born man is a husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
Subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [the sacred texts], he is purified in three years. When the sun has set, [if he touches] a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or a woman...
How is purification prescribed for one who touches a woman who has recently given birth?
By looking at fire, gold, and the path of the moon.
Having bathed with the permission of a Brāhmaṇa, she becomes pure;
likewise, two Brāhmaṇa women who have become menstruating (rajasvalā) by touching one another [become pure after bathing].

She should remain without food for that long; she becomes pure after three nights alone. If two women—one a Brāhmaṇī and the other a Kṣatriyā—touch each other while in their menstrual period, the former shall perform an Ardha-Kṛcchra penance, and the latter a single Pāda.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, touch one another, [they must perform penance].

If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch each other, she who is of Brāhmaṇa birth shall perform the penance prescribed for the preceding case, while the other shall perform one-quarter of that penance.
A woman previously married to a Śūdra is purified by a Kṛcchra penance and by giving a gift;
however, a menstruating woman who has bathed becomes pure on the fourth day.
One should perform rites for the gods, the ancestors, and so forth upon the cessation of the menstrual flow;
however, that which is the menses of women flows daily due to disease.
She does not become impure by that [menstrual flow], and therefore it is considered to be a time for eating only once a day; she should remain virtuous in her conduct as long as the flow continues.
When the menstrual flow has ceased, a woman is fit to be approached; indeed, she is engaged in household duties.
On the first day [of her period], she is like a Caṇḍālī; on the second day, she is a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
On the third day she is called a washerwoman, and on the fourth day she becomes pure. When a bath is required for one who is ill, a healthy person should bathe ten times.
Having bathed repeatedly, he should touch him; then that afflicted person shall become pure.
A twice-born man who has been touched by one who is impure from eating, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra, [should act likewise].
By fasting for one night, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Upon being touched by a Śūdra who is not rendered impure by food remnants, bathing is prescribed.
If one is touched by that leavings, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance;
bell-metal is purified by ashes, provided it has not been smeared with liquor.
Anything touched by even a trace of *surā* is purified by heating over fire and scraping;
likewise, vessels of white brass (*kāṃsya*) that have been smelled by a cow or defiled by one's own crow [are purified in the same manner].
Those things which are the leavings of a Śūdra are purified by ten alkaline substances;
likewise, after rinsing the mouth and performing the cleansing of the feet, vessels made of bell-metal (kāṃsya) are purified.
Having buried iron [objects] in the ground for six months and then having extracted them, one should bring them back;
for iron items and those made of lead, purification is performed in fire.
Teeth, bone, as well as beeswax, silver, golden vessels, and bowls made of gems or stone— these one should cleanse with water.
Furthermore, for stone, purification is declared to be by scrubbing;
for earthenware, purification is by burning, and for grains, it is also by winnowing.
The purification of bamboo, bark, rags, linen, cotton cloth, woolen blankets,
and silken cloths is held to be by sprinkling.
For muñja grass, household utensils, winnowing baskets, hemp, fruits, skins, straw, wood, and ropes, sprinkling with water is prescribed as the method of purification.
Cotton mattresses and other bedding, as well as red garments and the like,
reach purity by being dried in the sun and then sprinkled with water.
Manu has declared that cats, flies, insects, moths, worms, and frogs— even when they touch pure or impure things— do not cause one to become defiled by leavings.
Water that has reached the ground after touching it, as well as mutual droplets [from one person to another],
food remnants, and likewise oily substances— Manu declared these not to be *ucchiṣṭa* (ritual impurity from eating).

Regarding betel, sugarcane, fruit, after eating, after applying oil or ointments, at the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), and during the Soma sacrifice— the wise know that, according to dharma, these are not considered "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa).
Roads, mud, water, boats, paths,
and grass are purified by the wind and the sun, as are structures built of baked bricks.
A continuous stream that is not impure, dust raised by the wind,
women, the elderly, and children— these are never defiled.
In the event of the ruin of one's country, during exile, or even in times of disease or calamity,
one should certainly protect one's own body and so forth first, and thereafter practice dharma.

By whatever means possible—whether mild or harsh—one should rescue oneself from distress; once capable, one should practice dharma. But when the time of calamity has passed, one should attend to the rules of purification and proper conduct.
Afterwards, having attained purification, one who is restored to health should practice the Dharma.
(ParSm 7.38cd) If death should occur unintentionally while [cattle] are tied to their tethering ropes, what expiation shall there be for a sin committed unintentionally? (ParSm 8.1)
One should confess one's own sin to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who understand the treatises on dharma, and who are devoted to their own prescribed duties.
Those Brahmins who, out of ignorance, neglect the Sāvitrī and the Gāyatrī, the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsti), and the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
are merely tillers of the soil and bearers of the name "Brahmin."
For those who observe no vows, who do not know the mantras, and who subsist merely by their caste—
even if they are assembled in their thousands— no assembly (pariṣad) exists.
Whatever those who are deluded by darkness, fools, and ignorant of dharma proclaim as dharma—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who spoke it.
He who prescribes an expiation without having understood the treatises on Dharma becomes purified through that very act of expiation, while the guilt shall fall upon the assembly.
Whether four or even three who have mastered the Vedas should declare something,
that is to be known as Dharma, and not so by thousands of others.
Sin trembles before those who speak of the true qualities of reality, who proclaim the Dharma while seeking the path that is the means of valid knowledge.
Just as water situated within a stone is purified by the wind and the sun,
even so, by the instruction of the assembly, one should cause his evil deed to vanish.
The sin does not go to the perpetrator, nor does it go to the assembly;
through contact with wind, the sun, and so forth, the sin perishes like water.
Whether there be four or even three Brāhmaṇas who are knowers of the Vedas, performers of the Agnihotra sacrifice, and capable [in their duties], that assembly is so designated.
Those others who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and are knowers of the Dharma— whether five or three— such an assembly is proclaimed as a *pariṣad*.
Even a single person may constitute an assembly (*pariṣad*) for those sages who know the self, for the twice-born who perform sacrifices, and for those who have been initiated into the Vedic vows.
Five [kinds of assemblies] were previously mentioned by me; in their absence, there are three. That assembly which consists of those who are satisfied with their own livelihood is proclaimed as such.
But those Brahmins who, from this point forward, are merely bearers of the name—
there is no status as an assembly among them, even if they are multiplied by a thousand.
Just as an elephant made of wood, and just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
As a village site is empty, as a well is without water,
and as an oblation offered into a non-fire, so is a Brāhmaṇa who lacks the sacred mantras.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a barren cow is fruitless,
and just as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied the Rigveda fruitless.
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by various parts,
so too is Brahminhood produced by means of purificatory rites preceded by mantras.
Those twice-born who merely bear the name of a Brahmin and prescribe penance [for those who do not deserve it],
being performers of sinful deeds, have all gone together to hell.
Those twice-born who recite the Veda and those who are devoted to the five sacrifices—
they rescue the three worlds, even if they are attached to the five senses.
A fire well-kindled in cremation grounds is a consumer of all things;
likewise, a Brahmin learned in the Vedas is a deity, even if he consumes all things.
Just as all impure things are cast into water,
even so, O twice-born one, should one cast all sin into the fire.
A Brahmin devoid of the Gāyatrī becomes more impure even than a Śūdra;
those twice-born ones who know the reality of Brahman through the Gāyatrī are honored by people.
Even a twice-born man of evil character is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses.
Who would abandon a cow, however wicked, and instead milk a she-ass, even if it were well-trained?
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas,
are said to represent the supreme Dharma in whatever they declare, even if spoken in jest.
One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), a reciter of the Dharma,
and three from the principal stages of life (*āśrama*)— this assembly (*parṣad*) consists of at least ten members.
Having remained with the king's consent, he should prescribe the penance (*prāyaścitta*);
he must not act on his own authority, but rather a small expiation (*niṣkṛti*) should be performed.
If a king, bypassing those Brāhmaṇas, desires to do something [unjust],
that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after the king.
One should always perform the penance (prāyaścitta) in front of a deity’s sanctuary;
having then undergone the Kṛcchra penance for oneself, one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas (the Gāyatrī).
Having shaved his hair along with the top-knot, he should bathe at the three junctions of the day;
he should dwell among cows at night and follow them during the day.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first providing protection for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or that of others, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking.
One should drink water while [women] are drinking, and one should lie down while they are lying down;
one should rescue with all one's strength a woman who has fallen or is mired in the mud.
He who gives up his life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa,
as is the protector of a cow or of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should prescribe a Prājāpatya penance in proportion to the value of the cattle;
that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra is then divided into four types.
For one day he shall eat only a single meal; for one day he shall eat only at night;
for one day he shall eat only what is unasked for; and for one day he shall subsist on air alone.
For two days he should eat only one meal a day, for two days he should eat his single meal at the normal time;
for two days he should live on alms, and for two days he should subsist on air alone.
For three days he should eat only one meal a day; for three days he should eat only at night;
for three days he should be a non-seeker of alms (fasting); and for three days his sustenance should be air alone.
For four days he should eat only one meal a day; for four days he should eat only at night;
for four days he should not beg for food; and for four days he should subsist on air alone.
When the penance has been performed, one should then provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas;
the twice-born should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas and recite purificatory prayers (pavitra).
Having fed Brāhmaṇas, the cow-killer is purified without a doubt. For the sake of protecting cows, one does not incur sin through confining or tethering them;
likewise, one should not consider that as a killing, whether done intentionally or unintentionally.
If one should cause [an ox] to fall by means other than a blow from a staff,
then the penance prescribed for killing a cow must be performed twice over.
Confinement, binding, yoking, and striking—these constitute the fourfold [punishment].
One should undergo one quarter of the penance for confinement, and two quarters for binding.

In other cases, the penance shall be reduced by one quarter; however, in the case of killing [a cow], one must perform the full penance—whether it occurs in a cow-pen, in a house, in a difficult place, or on uneven ground.
Now, in rivers, in oceans, and in other [waters] except at their mouths,
cows that die in a scorched region are said to be obstructed by a dam.

If a cow dies while tied up at home or even in the forest with a yoke-tie, a tethering rope, a halter, or ornaments such as necklaces and other decorations; ||| ParSm09-6cd ||| [then the following applies].
One should know that very same act as a binding offense, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally,
when one is oppressed by men with a plough, a cart, a row [of oxen], or on the back.
The owner of the ox incurs death, and the yoktra becomes of that same nature;
whether he be intoxicated, careless, insane, conscious, or even unconscious.
Whether done intentionally or unintentionally, one may strike with sticks or stones out of anger;
whether the victim is struck or even killed, that [anger] is indeed the cause of the downfall.
If, however, he has fainted or fallen, or has been struck by a staff,
and when he rises and proceeds [to the ordeal], whether after five, seven, or even ten steps,
or if he should take a mouthful of food or drink water, [he is declared innocent].
If one was already afflicted by disease prior [to the offense], no penance is prescribed.
If one kills an embryo while it is still in the form of a *piṇḍa*, the penance is one quarter; if it is measured as being in the stage of a *garbha*, it is two quarters;
for killing an insentient embryo, the vow is declared to be less than a quarter.

For a minor limb (pāda), there is the shaving of the hair on the body; for two parts (dvi-pāda), the beard as well; for three parts (tri-pāda), however, everything except the top-knot (śikhā); but in the case of a total downfall (nipātana), including the top-knot.
For a quarter [of the offense], a pair of garments; for two quarters, a bronze vessel;
for three quarters, one should give a bull; for four quarters, it is prescribed that two cows be given.
But if one who has all his limbs fully developed is seen to be unconscious,
yet complete in every major and minor limb, he shall perform the cow-vow (go-vrata) for double the duration.
If cows are struck by means of a stone or a staff,
one should perform a quarter-penance (*pāda*) for breaking a horn, and two quarters for injuring an eye.
If cows are struck by means of a stone or a staff,
one should perform one quarter-penance (pāda) for breaking a horn, and two quarters for injuring an eye.
For breaking a tail, one should perform a quarter *kṛcchra*; for fracturing a bone, two quarters;
for [breaking] an ear, three quarters; and for severing it entirely, one should perform the full penance.
In the case of breaking a horn, breaking a bone, or likewise breaking the hip—
if he survives for six months, no penance is prescribed.
When a wound has been treated, anointing with oil should be performed by hand;
and fodder should be brought for him until he has regained his full strength.
As long as all its limbs are complete, so long should a man nourish it;
having bowed before a Brahmin in the form of a cow, he should dismiss it.
If, however, one whose limbs are incomplete or whose body is deficient should become a killer of a cow,
then one should prescribe an expiation for that person on his behalf.
One who, having exerted force, kills a cow with wood, clods of earth, stones, or even with a weapon— for him,
one should prescribe purification.
One should perform the Sāṃtapana penance for killing a wooden post, the Prājāpatya for a clod of earth,
the Tapta-kṛcchra for a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for a weapon.
In the Pañcasaṃtapanaka penance, there are five cows; likewise, in the Prājāpatya, there are three. In the Tapta-kṛcchra, there are eight cows, and in the Atikṛcchra, there are thirteen.
"In the case of killing living beings, one should give a substitute for it, or its equivalent value; thus spoke Manu. (Parāśara Smṛti 9.26)
Except for branding and marking, as well as for the purpose of releasing the animal,
and for the sake of its protection at night, one does not incur sin by confining or tethering it.
In cases of excessive burning, excessive carrying [of loads], as well as piercing the nose,
and when crossing rivers or mountains, one should prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

If one burns [a tree] excessively, one should perform one quarter of the penance; if one cuts it down for transport, one should perform two quarters; if one cuts it at the nose, one should perform three-quarters; but if one fells it entirely, one should perform the full penance.
"But if an ox yoked with a harness dies from exhaustion,
it has been stated by Parāśara that one foot [of the penance] is prescribed according to the rule."
Confinement, binding, carrying burdens, striking, driving through difficult terrain, and the use of a tether— these six are the causes of death.
If a cow dies while its limbs are well-restrained by a tether or a rope within the owner's house,
the owner becomes a sinner and deserves half of the prescribed penance.
[A cow] should not be bound with coconut fibers, nor with hemp fibers, nor even with muñja grass, nor with ropes made of bark.
Cows should not be tied up with these [materials]; even if they are bound, one should remain standing while holding onto another living being.
One should bind a cow or a calf with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, facing the south. There is no expiation for those [cows] burnt by fire that was attached to the tethering rope.
If wood should be present there, how can there be an expiation?
By reciting the purifying goddess, one is released from that sin.
By driving [cattle] into wells or tanks, by causing them to fall during the felling of trees,
by selling them fodder, or by otherwise neglecting them, one incurs the same sin as the killing of a cow.
But when anyone who has been honored is found with a broken limb,
or with his ear or heart pierced, or submerged in a well or a narrow pit;
And likewise, when one falls from a well, or when there is a fracture of the neck or the legs,
and he dies there, one should perform three-quarters of the penance. This applies also in the case of digging a well, constructing an embankment, building a river-dam, or at water-stations (prapās).
For those who have perished in water, no expiation is prescribed.
In the case of digging a well, a pit, a pond, or likewise a long trench,
as well as in other dharma-pits (dharmakhāta), no expiation is prescribed.
If a man desires to dig a pit at the entrance of a house or in his dwellings— for his own business or for the excavation of a house— one should prescribe an expiation for such acts.
For those who have died while fasting as part of a religious vow, or those killed by serpents or tigers,
or those perished by fire or lightning, no penance is prescribed.
In the event of a village being destroyed, by a flood of water, or by the collapse of a house,
and for those killed by excessive rain, no expiation is prescribed.
For those killed in battle, those who have perished in cremation fires,
and those killed by forest fires or in village massacres, no penance is prescribed.
If a cow is restrained for the purpose of medical treatment or for the delivery of a dead fetus,
and she dies despite every effort being made, no penance is prescribed.
One should prescribe an expiation for many people who have died while being bound or confined,
as well as for a physician who has administered false treatment.
In the event of the death of cows or bulls, all those people who were looking on and did not attempt to prevent it shall incur the sin.
If a single person is killed by many acting together and it is not known whose blow caused his death,
the slayer must be identified through divine ordeal by those appointed by the king, and then removed from society.
If a single woman is killed by many people through some accident,
they shall each perform one quarter of the penance for killing separately.
If [the victim] is killed, blood is visible; if seized by disease, he becomes emaciated;
if bitten, saliva appears—thus should the investigation proceed.
Even when urged for the sake of a morsel of food, he does not go on his way;
thus has Manu alone, who knows all the scriptures, declared.
The expiation prescribed by him for a cow-killer is that he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
however, for the sake of preserving his hair, he should perform double the vow.
When a vow is prescribed as being double [the usual], the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be double;
whether it be a king, a prince, or a Brāhmaṇa of great learning.
If one has not performed the shaving [of the head], one should prescribe an expiation for him:
having pulled out all the hair, one should have two finger-breadths cut off.
In this manner, the shaving of the head is prescribed for women and young girls; however, there is no shaving of the hair for a woman, nor should she sleep or eat at a distance [from her husband].
One should not stay overnight in a cow-pen, nor should one follow cows during the day,
especially at river confluences and in forests.
For women, there is no deer-skin or [specific] garment; they should simply observe the vow.
It is said that they must likewise perform bathing at the three junctions of the day and the worship of the gods.
In the midst of their kinsmen, their penance shall consist of the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such observances;
they should remain constantly in their homes and practice purity with strict discipline.
He who, having committed the slaughter of a cow in this world, desires to conceal it,
goes without doubt to the terrible hell known as Kālasūtra.
Released from that hell, that man is born in the world of mortals as a eunuch,
a sufferer, and a leper for seven births.
Therefore, one should not cause harm to others; one should constantly practice one's own duty (*svadharma*).
One should avoid excessive anger toward women, children, servants, cattle, and Brahmins.
I shall now declare the means of atonement (*niṣkṛti*) that is beneficial for all members of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*).
And for approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification.

One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight; on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should indeed determine the size of the morsel to be equal to a hen's egg;
otherwise, through the fault of improper state, there is neither dharma nor purification.
After that penance has been performed, one should provide a meal for a Brahmin;
one should give two cows and a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
If a twice-born man approaches a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī,
he shall fast for three nights, following the instruction of the Brahmins.
Having performed the purificatory rite with the topknot intact, one should perform two Prājāpatya penances;
Pārāśara has declared that one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee for purification.
If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should have sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman,
he should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give away two pairs of cattle.
If a Śūdra has sexual intercourse with a woman who cooks for herself or with a Caṇḍālī,
he shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of four cows.
If one should have sexual intercourse with his mother, a sister, or likewise his own daughter—
if, being deluded, he has approached these women, he shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
One should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances; by cutting one's hair while bathing, one becomes pure.
And likewise, for sexual intercourse with one's mother's sister, there shall be the excision of one's own penis.
But he who should go [to her] through ignorance shall perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
Pārāśara has declared that he attains purification by giving ten pairs of cows and bulls.
Having ascended upon the wife of one's father, or the daughter of one's mother’s kinsman, or the wife of one's teacher, or a daughter-in-law, or likewise the wife of one's brother; ParSm 10.12cd.
One who has sexual intercourse with his maternal aunt or a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā) shall perform three Prājāpatya penances;
he should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and he is thereby purified—of this there is no doubt.
Upon approaching a cow, a female slave, and so forth, as well as a buffalo, a female camel, a female monkey,
a female donkey, or a female pig, one should observe the Prājāpatya vow.

One who has sexual intercourse with a cow is purified by a three-night fast and by giving one cow to a Brāhmaṇa; however, one who has intercourse with a buffalo, a female camel, or a she-ass is purified by a single day and night.
In a riot, in battle, during a famine, or in a time of mass destruction of people;
when captured as a prisoner, or when afflicted by fear—one should always look upon one's own wife.
If a woman maintains contact with Caṇḍālas,
she should then have ten Brahmins summoned and confess her own fault.
In a pit dug up to the neck, filled with cow-dung, water, and mud,
one should remain there without food for a day and night and then emerge. Having shaved the hair including the top-knot, one should eat only barley-gruel.
Having fasted for three nights, one should dwell in water for one night.
Having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *saṅkhapuṣpī* creeper,
along with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should drink the water.
Thereafter, she should subsist on a single meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
as long as she performs that vow, for that long she dwells outside [the community].
"When the penance has thus been performed, one should feed Brāhmaṇas and give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
Pārāśara has declared this to be purification."
For women of the four castes, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa are the prescribed vows.
As is the earth, so is a woman; therefore, one should not defile her.
If a woman has been enjoyed by force—having been captured as a prisoner, killed, bound, or through fear—she is purified by performing the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance; so said Pārāśara.
But a woman who has been enjoyed once by sinful acts against her will is purified by the Prājāpatya penance and by menstruation.
Half of the body of that man falls [into ruin] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is ordained.
While muttering the Gāyatrī, one should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance.
[The ingredients are] the Gāyatrī, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, Kuśa grass water, and...
A fast for one night is recorded as the *sāṃtapana* *kṛcchra*.
[This applies to a woman] who conceives a child by a paramour when her husband has died, or when he is unaccounted for or has gone abroad.
One should abandon her in another kingdom if she is fallen and a doer of evil; but when a Brāhmaṇa woman goes forth associated with another man, [she must be abandoned].
But she who, out of lust or delusion, goes [to another man] having abandoned her kinsmen, children, and husband, is declared lost; there is no returning for her again.
But that woman who, overcome by intoxication and delusion, has been struck with a staff or other weapons out of anger, is lost in the next world, especially among human beings.
Even if she has gone with another, there shall be a return [to her husband];
when the tenth day arrives, no penance is required.
For ten days one should not abandon the woman, nor should one abandon her when her menses have ceased;
the husband shall perform the Kṛcchra penance, and his kinsmen half of that Kṛcchra.
Having eaten from or drunk from those [vessels], one is purified after a day and night; but when a Brāhmaṇī woman, being free from desire, has intercourse with another man...
Having approached [a woman], she goes to a hundred men; therefore, the kinsmen of her lineage should abandon her. If a man should go to [her] in the house, then that house becomes impure.
Whether it be the house of the husband, the mother, or the house of the paramour—
having first scraped that house, one should subsequently sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

One should discard an earthen vessel, but one should purify cloth and wood. All ritual implements made of fruit-wood should be purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with cow-hair.

Copper vessels [should be purified] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and bell-metal vessels with ten applications of ash; the Brāhmaṇa should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) as prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and perform two Prājāpatya penances.
For others, purification consists of fasting for one day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Through fasts, meritorious vows, ritual bathing, twilight devotions, worship, and so forth, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, compassion, and charity, the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are purified.
Space, wind, fire, water on the ground,
and *darbha* grass do not become impure, just as the *camasa* cups do not [become impure] during sacrifices.
Impure semen, beef, or even the food of a *caṇḍāla*— [these do not defile].
If, however, it has been eaten by a Brahmin, he should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
In the same way, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should also perform half a Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
and when a Śūdra eats [forbidden food] in this manner, he should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while a twice-born man should drink the Brahmakūrca.
He should give one, two, three, or four cows, respectively, according to the order starting with the Brāhmaṇa.
The food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), and the food of one whose food is unfit to be eaten;
likewise, food of doubtful origin, prohibited food, and likewise the leavings of another—these should not be consumed.
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food] out of ignorance or due to distress, he should,
upon realizing it, perform the purifying Brahmakūrca penance.
When food has been defiled by the presence of children, mongooses, or cats, it is purified by sprinkling it with water containing sesame seeds and *darbha* grass; there is no doubt in this matter.
When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a communal meal,
if even one person should set aside his vessel, the remaining food must not be eaten.
If a Brahmin should, out of delusion, eat the leavings of food from that row,
he must perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Sāṃtapana penance as expiation.
Pīyūṣa (the milk of a cow within seven days of calving), white garlic, the fruit of the vṛntāka,
gṛñjana, onion, the resin of trees, and mushrooms that grow on sacred ground.
If a twice-born man consumes camel’s milk or ewe’s milk through ignorance,
he becomes pure by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having eaten a frog as well as the flesh of a mouse,
a Brahmin who has learned [of the act] is purified by subsisting on barley-gruel for a day and a night.
A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are diligent in their duties and pure in their observances—
in the house of such persons, food may always be eaten by the twice-born for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Clarified butter, oil, as well as milk and food cooked with fat—
a Brahmin who has gone to the bank of a river and eats such food [is considered to be] eating the food of a Śūdra.
