A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is constantly addicted to liquor and meat and who engages in base occupations, just as he would avoid his own cooked food.
A twice-born man should never abandon those Śūdras who are devoted to serving the twice-born, who abstain from liquor and meat, and who are constantly intent upon their own duties.
If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka),
how should one prescribe the expiation (prāyaścitta) for them in each respective caste?
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times; for a Vaiśya, it is by five thousand, and for a Kṣatriya, by three thousand.
When a Brāhmaṇa eats [the food of such a person], he should cause two thousand [cows] to be given;
or else, he is purified by a single recitation of the Vāmadevya Sāman.
Manu has declared that dry food, cow's milk, and fats obtained from the house of a Śūdra are fit to be eaten if they have been cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
If a Brahmin has eaten in the house of a Śūdra during times of distress,
he shall be purified by mental remorse or by reciting the Drupadā verse one hundred times.
A slave, a barber, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who shares half the harvest—
these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
A son begotten by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Śūdra maiden, if he is consecrated with the sacraments, becomes a Dāsa; if he is not consecrated with the sacraments, he becomes a Nāpita.
The son born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra maiden is to be known as a Gopāla; he may be fed by Brahmins, without a doubt.
A son born from a Vaiśya maiden who has been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa is to be known as an Ārdhika; he may be fed by Brāhmaṇas without any doubt.
If one unintentionally consumes water, curd, ghee, or milk that has been kept in vessels belonging to those whose food is forbidden to eat,
what should the expiation be?
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who approaches [for sexual intercourse],
the expiation for one of the twice-born castes is the Brahmakūrca fast.
For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra becomes pure through giving.
A *brahmakūrca* fast for a day and night purifies even one who cooks his own food.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kūśa* grass—
this is designated as the *pañcagavya*, which is purifying and a cleanser of sins.
Cow urine [is taken] from a black cow, and cow dung from a white one;
milk is taken from a copper-colored cow, and curd from a red one.
Ghee from a tawny cow (kapilā) should be taken, or indeed all [ghee] from a tawny cow;
one should give one *pala* of urine and half the size of an elephant’s thumb of cow dung.
One should give seven palas of milk, three palas of curd are prescribed,
one pala of ghee should be given, and one pala of kuśa-water.
Having taken cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with the verse beginning "gandhadvārām," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhi krāvṇaḥ."

With the mantra "tejo 'si" (you are luster), one should prepare the clarified butter (*ājya*); with "śukram asi" (you are semen), the *kuśa*-water; and with "devasya tvā," the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Having purified these with the *ṛc*, one should place them in the vicinity of the fire.
Having stirred [the water] with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should recite over it the mantra "mānastoke.
Furthermore, those *darbha* blades which are at least seven in number, with uncut tips and white luster, [are to be used].
Having extracted these [five products of the cow], one should offer the *pañcagavya* according to the rule,
with the mantras "Irāvatī," "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "Mā nas toke," and the *śaṃvatī*.
With these [mantras] the oblation must be offered, and the twice-born should drink the remainder of what was offered,
having stirred it with the *praṇava* and churned it with the *praṇava*.
Having drawn [the water] up with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink it with the *praṇava*;
for whatever sin residing in the bones remains within the bodies of embodied beings.
The Brahmakūrca destroys everything, just as a blazing fire consumes fuel;
it is a purifier in the three worlds, presided over by the deities.
Varuṇa resides in cow urine, and the bearer of oblations (Agni) in cow dung;
Vāyu is declared to be in curd, Soma in milk, and the Sun in clarified butter.
One should know that water which has fallen from the mouth into a vessel while someone is drinking is unfit to be drunk; having drunk it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a twice-born man sees a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
or if he drinks water that has fallen [into it] along with bones, skin, and other such impurities, he becomes impure.
A human corpse, a crow, a village pig, a donkey, a camel,
a gavaya, a supratīka, a peacock, and likewise a rhinoceros;
If one sinks into a well belonging to a Vaiyyāghra, an Ārkṣa, or a Siṃha, or if one has drunk the water of a defiled pond; 11.43cd.
By this entire sequence, the expiation for a man shall be determined in its entirety.
A Brahmin becomes purified in three nights, while a Kṣatriya is purified in two days.
A Vaiśya, however, becomes pure in one day, while a Śūdra becomes pure by eating only at night.
Of one who has turned away from cooking for others, and of one who is devoted to cooking for others.
A twice-born man who eats the food of an outcaste (apaca) shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
as for the gift given by an outcaste, how can there be any fruit for the donor?
Both the giver and the receiver—these two go to hell.
Having taken the fire and established it, one must not fail to perform the five sacrifices.
He who abstains from cooking for others is proclaimed by the sages as one who lives on the food of others, having himself performed the five great sacrifices.
That Brahmin who, having constantly risen early in the morning, is devoted to the food of others and is devoid of the duties of a householder, [is a sinner].
The sages who knew the true essence of dharma have proclaimed the duties of the various castes; for in every age, there are specific duties corresponding to the brahmins of those respective times.
One must not utter censure against them, for those twice-born ones are the very form of the Yugas.
Having uttered the sound "hum" to a Brāhmaṇa, or the word "thou" to a superior one, [one must perform penance].

Having bathed, he should remain standing for the remainder of the day; having offered salutations, he should propitiate [the person he has offended], even if he has struck him with a blade of grass or bound him by the neck with a garment.
Even after winning a legal dispute, one should appease the opponent by bowing down;
however, for threatening him, the penance is one day and night, and for striking him against the ground, it is three nights.

In the case of blood [discharge], one should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance; when there is internal bleeding, the *kṛcchra*. For nine days, one should subsist on a handful of food as part of the *atikṛcchra*.
One who fasts for three nights is said to perform the *atikṛcchra*;
this is prescribed when a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred.

The Gāyatrī, when practiced ten thousand times, is the supreme means of purification. If one sees a bad dream, or after vomiting, or after the rite of shaving, or after sexual intercourse, or from the smoke of a funeral pyre, bathing alone is prescribed.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or that which has been touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of regeneration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
The deerskin, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born at the time of the rite of re-consecration.
One who eats feces or urine shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for purification;
having bathed, one who has become impure through drinking [such substances] shall consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Regarding those who have committed suicide by water or fire, those who have entered the life of a wandering mendicant, and those who have lost their caste—
how is the purification of such outcasts prescribed?
By two *prājāpatya* penances, by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
and by the gift of eleven bulls, those three castes are purified.
I shall declare [the penance] for a Brāhmaṇa: having gone to the forest at a crossroads and shaved his head together with the topknot, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances.

"One should give two cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); Svāyambhuva has declared that this brings about purification. By means of that, one is released from the sin and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa."
The wise have proclaimed five meritorious types of bathing:
the fiery (āgneya), the watery (vāruṇa), the brāhma, the windy (vāyavya), and the celestial (divya).

The *āgneya* bath is performed with ashes; the *vāruṇa* bath is by immersing oneself in water; the *brāhma* bath is performed with the hymn beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the *vāyavya* bath is traditionally defined as [bathing in] the dust raised by cows.
That which is performed by means of rain accompanied by sunshine is called a divine bath (*divya-snāna*);
having bathed therein, a person becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā.
All the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, follow a twice-born man who goes to bathe;
they move along in the form of air, afflicted by thirst and seeking water.
When the wringing out of the cloth is performed, they turn back disappointed;
therefore, one should not wring out the cloth without having first performed the libation to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa).
He who, having placed [sesame] in the pores of his skin, offers libations to the ancestors with sesame seeds—
by him the ancestors are satisfied with that blood and that filth.
A twice-born man who shakes his hair after bathing, or who discharges impurity while bathing,
or even one who sips water while standing in the water, is excluded from the rites of the ancestors and the gods.
Having covered the head or the neck, or even with the lower garment tucked up or the topknot untied,
or without the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), one becomes impure even after sipping water (*ācamana*).

One standing in water should not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) while remaining in the water, nor should one standing on land do so while remaining on land. Having touched both [water and land], one who has performed the sipping becomes pure in both places.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and having put on a different garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
Upon sneezing, spitting, having food remnants on the teeth, speaking untruth,
or conversing with those who have fallen from their caste, one should touch the right ear.
"Prabhāsa and other sacred fords (*tīrtha*), as well as the Gaṅgā and other rivers,
reside within the right ear of a Brahmin," so Manu has declared.
Fire, water, the Vedas, as well as Soma, the Sun, and the Wind [reside there].
But all [the fires] of a Brahmin stand on the right side, following the current.
Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised;
bathing at night is not recommended, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [an eclipse].
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and burnt offerings should be performed during an eclipse of Rāhu;
on other occasions, however, the night is impure, therefore one should avoid it.
The Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are the deities; they all dissolve into Soma; therefore, a gift [should be made] during its eclipse.

At a threshing-floor sacrifice, at a wedding, at the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign, and likewise during an eclipse, as well as on the *sarvayā* day, the giving of gifts is indeed prescribed; it is not ordained for any other occasion.

At the birth of a son, at a sacrifice, and likewise at a rite for averting calamity, as well as upon the sight of Rāhu [during an eclipse], giving is praised; it is not so at other times, nor during the night.
The two middle watches of the night should be known as the "great night" (mahāniśā). During the first and last watches, one should perform the bath as prescribed for the day.
A sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a caṇḍāla, and a seller of soma [are places where bathing is forbidden].
Having touched these, however, a Brāhmaṇa should enter the water with his clothes on.
Before the collection of the bones, one should perform a bath after weeping;
for a Brahmin who dies within ten days, however, there shall be only sipping of water (ācamana) once that period has passed.
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, water is equal to the Gaṅgā in every respect;
the same has been declared regarding the moon’s eclipse with respect to rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts.
When a twice-born man performs a bath purified by *kuśa* grass, or sips water with *kuśa*,
or uses water drawn up with *kuśa*, it becomes equal to the drinking of Soma.
Those who have fallen away from the fire-rituals, those who have abandoned the worship of the twilights (saṃdhyā),
and those who do not study the Veda— all these are declared to be *vṛṣalas*.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who is especially afraid of a low-born man (vṛṣala) should study at least a portion [of the Veda],
even if he is unable to study it all.
Even for one who studies constantly, or performs recitations and burnt offerings, if he is nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food,
no higher state exists for him.
The food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra,
and even the acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra— these will cause one to fall, even if one is blazing with spiritual merit.
That twice-born man who constantly cooks for a Śūdra woman and whose housewife is a Śūdra woman,
being excluded from the rites for the ancestors and the gods, goes to the Raurava hell.
A twice-born man who has grown fat on the food of a Śūdra while undergoing impurity due to death or birth,
saying "I do not know this," what various wombs shall he go to?
For twelve births he becomes a vulture, for ten births a pig,
and for seven births he remains in his own species— thus Manu has declared.
If a Brahmin who accepts gifts from a Śūdra should offer the oblation for that Śūdra,
the Brahmin becomes a Śūdra, and the Śūdra becomes a Brahmin.
Having undertaken the vow of silence, the twice-born man should remain seated and not speak. For if he should speak while eating, one must avoid that food.
If a Brahmin drinks water from that vessel while half of the meal remains uneaten,
he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and brings ruin upon himself.
But among the Brahmins who are eating, he who first sets down his vessel is a fool and a most sinful man; indeed, he is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
When the vessels are still standing, those twice-born who pronounce "svasti" [without first performing the formal dismissal],
the gods do not attain satisfaction, and likewise the ancestors depart disappointed.
One should never eat without having bathed, without having muttered prayers, without having offered oblations into the fire,
nor on the back of a leaf, nor at night without a lamp.
But the householder, endowed with compassion, should reflect only upon dharma;
being of sound intellect and abiding in justice, he should do so for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those dependent on him.
One must indeed protect oneself with wealth acquired through righteous means;
however, he who lives by unrighteous means is excluded from all religious rites.

One who has maintained the sacred fire, a tawny cow, one who performs a long sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should look upon them constantly.
One should keep these things in the house: the two fire-drills, a black cat, sandalwood, a fine gem, clarified butter, sesame seeds, a black antelope skin, and a goat.
Where a hundred cows with one bull remain unrestrained,
that field, multiplied tenfold, is proclaimed to be a *go-carma*.
A mortal [is purified] from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, by the gift of this ox-hide; he is liberated from all taints.
A gift that is given specifically to a poor family man who is learned in the Vedas brings about auspicious merit.
One who seizes land is not purified by the construction of step-wells, wells, tanks, and the like, nor by hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, nor even by the gift of ten million cows.
Before eighteen days have passed, a menstruating woman must simply bathe;
beyond that, she must observe a three-night period of impurity—so the sage Uśanas declared.

One yuga, two yugas, three yugas, and four yugas [are the periods of impurity] for a Cāṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and one who has fallen from grace, respectively.
Then, by mere proximity, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
having bathed, if one has touched [the corpse] through ignorance, one should gaze at the sun.
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge,
drinks water with his mouth when [purifying substances] are available in his hand, he will certainly be born in his own womb (as a dog).
But if a man, out of anger, should declare his wife to be unapproachable,
yet later desires her again, he must have it proclaimed in the midst of Brahmins.
One who is exhausted, angry, blinded by darkness, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear—
if such a person fails to perform a meritorious gift, the penance is three days.
One should perform ritual ablutions (upaspṛśet) three times a day at the confluence of great rivers. At the conclusion of the penance, one should give a cow as a gift and feed ten Brahmins.
Having eaten the food of a Brahmin of evil conduct or one who practices forbidden acts, a twice-born man shall fast for one day.
By eating the food of a Brahmin who follows the conduct of the virtuous and likewise knows the Upanishads,
a man is freed from sin within a day and night.
For eating food that is defiled by being above the rim, below the rim, or from the interior [of a vessel],
as well as during the menstrual period, or likewise upon the death of one who is impure, one should perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
A kṛcchra penance, ten thousand recitations of the Devī-mantra, two hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), and twelve ritual baths at a sacred ford while the head remains unwetted.
For a householder who intentionally causes the emission of semen upon the ground, a single Kṛcchra penance is prescribed for every two Yojanas traveled on a pilgrimage to a sacred ford.

One who has been endowed with the fourfold knowledge should, according to the rule, recite the mantra of the Goddess one thousand times along with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should prescribe going to the ocean or to a sacred embankment as the expiation;
on the path of that embankment, one should beg for alms from members of the four castes.
Having avoided those engaged in forbidden acts, [he should go] without an umbrella or shoes, thinking:
"I am indeed a doer of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins."
"I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms, a slayer of a Brahmin. He should dwell among herds of cows, in villages, or in cities.
In penance groves, at sacred fords, or by rivers and springs—
having gone to the ocean, he shall proclaim his sin in these places and [attain] merit.
Ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length,
it was constructed by Nala, acting under the command of Rāmacandra.
By seeing the Setu of the ocean, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having seen the Setu and purified in soul, one should plunge into the sea.
Or else, a king who is the lord of the earth should perform an Aśvamedha sacrifice when he has returned home and approaches for the purpose of residing there.
Accompanied by his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas;
furthermore, he should give one hundred cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those learned in the four Vedas.
By the grace of the Brahmins, however, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated.
Having killed a woman who is engaged in a *savana* (a ritual extraction of soma), one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-vrata*).
A twice-born man who drinks liquor should go to a river that flows to the ocean;
once he has performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, he should then provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas.
One should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmins;
having drunk liquor even once, one should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire.
Having himself stolen gold from a Brāhmaṇa, he then torments both himself in this world and in the next. (ParSm 12.77)
Taking a pestle, he should go to the presence of the king for execution;
then he attains purification, and he is released by the king.
But that which is done intentionally deserves a different form of punishment than death [for unintentional acts],
due to sitting together, sleeping together, traveling together, conversing together, or eating together.
For sins indeed pass away like a drop of oil upon water;
[the means for this are] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal rite (yāvaka), and likewise the Tulāpuruṣa.
Following after cows indeed destroys all sins. This is the *Pārāśara* treatise, consisting of five hundred verses augmented by ninety-two; it is a compendium of the Dharmaśāstra.

Just as the acts of Vedic study [are to be performed], so too is this treatise on Dharma. It must be studied with effort by one who is constantly intent on attaining heaven. [No Sūtra on Vyavahāra (only Parāśaramādhava)]
